title: How the New England Vampire Panics Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss New England vampire panics of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. They begin with the 'Yankee' Connecticut family cemetery excavation by state archaeologist Nick Bellantoni, where a coffin marked J.B. 1855 (per the hosts) was found smashed and the skeleton rearranged. Bellantoni consulted Rhode Island folklorist Michael Bell, who documented about eighty exhumations across New England. They cover the European roots of vampire folklore (upir, strigoi), the earliest known reference in a 1784 Connecticut Courant letter from Moses Holmes, and George Stetson's late-nineteenth-century study. The hosts explain that tuberculosis (consumption) drove the panics: families believed a dead relative was sapping the living, so they exhumed bodies, looked for fresh blood near the heart, and burned hearts to make ash tonics, or used other remedies such as flipping coffins or staking. Decomposition signs like bloating, receding skin and nails, and blood at the lips were misread as vampirism. The episode closes with the case of Mercy Brown in Exeter, Rhode Island, whose family members died of TB; her heart was burned in 1892, and a newspaper clipping about it was reportedly found among Bram Stoker's papers. A listener mail segment follows from a Venezuelan listener living in Chile about passport and identity problems.

segments.title: Connecticut lost graves and the J.B. coffin
segments.summary: Kids find old graves in Connecticut; state archaeologist Nick Bellantoni excavates a family cemetery and finds a smashed coffin with the skeleton rearranged.

segments.title: Michael Bell and the scope of New England vampire panics
segments.summary: Bellantoni consults folklorist Michael Bell, who explains the panics lasted into the late nineteenth century and documents about eighty exhumations across New England, including Rhode Island.

segments.title: George Stetson, Thoreau, and contemporary reactions
segments.summary: Stetson's late-nineteenth-century study documented the beliefs; contemporaries such as the Boston Daily Globe and Thoreau reacted with disbelief.

segments.title: European roots of vampire folklore
segments.summary: The hosts trace the vampire legend to European beliefs about upiers and strigoi, and the earliest known American reference, a 1784 Connecticut newspaper letter by Moses Holmes warning against a foreign quack doctor.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of tuberculosis.

segments.title: Tuberculosis as the root of the panic
segments.summary: The hosts argue tuberculosis, known as consumption, explains the panics: families believed a dead relative was draining the living, and TB spread through close households.

segments.title: Exhumation practices and remedies
segments.summary: Families dug up suspected vampires, looked for fresh blood near the heart, misread decomposition signs, and used remedies such as burning hearts, flipping coffins, and staking.

segments.title: Mercy Brown case in Exeter, Rhode Island
segments.summary: Mercy Brown's family lost several members to TB; in 1892 her body was exhumed, her heart and liver burned, and a newspaper article was reportedly later found among Bram Stoker's papers.

segments.title: Listener mail from Venezuela
segments.summary: A listener living in Chile describes passport and identity document problems for Venezuelans abroad, and the hosts respond.
